clue.text: Don't let the public know Hugh's half started to push off

indicators.note: the half-name starts the answer, coming before the other piece
only half of the name is wanted, so its back two letters go

parts.note: the name Hugh, whose first half is kept

indicators.note: push off reads as the word push knocked off its proper order, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cover-up: Hugh is told to clear off before the story gets out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' keeps HU of Hugh; 'off' turns PUSH into SHUP; 'started' means HU comes first. 'push off' looks like a dismissal, but it is the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep something secret from the public is to suppress it, an idiomatic phrasal verb for a cover-up.

clue.text: Those people responsible for article on Hurley's butt

parts.note: THE is the definite article

indicators.note: a butt is the end of something, so the last letter of the name is taken

parts.note: Elizabeth Hurley, the model and actress; her name ends in Y

explanation.surface: Somebody has to answer for the piece written about Liz Hurley's bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butt' looks like Hurley's bottom, a fair subject for the Eye, but here it means the end of her name.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun is used for unnamed authorities, as in 'they say', the people in charge.

clue.text: A tip: our Nigel's only half there

indicators.note: only half of the name is present, so the back four of its eight letters are dropped

parts.note: Private Eye's own nickname for the gossip columnist Nigel Dempster is Nigel Dumpster

explanation.surface: A hint that the Eye's favourite diarist is a bit dim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only half there' reads as calling Nigel dim; it actually keeps the first half of Dumpster, the Eye's name for Nigel Dempster of the Daily Mail diary.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip is a rubbish heap, and so is a dump, both places where waste is left.

clue.text: Obsessive anxiety? So insure, stupid!

indicators.note: stupid suggests the words have been thrown into a senseless jumble, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An exasperated broker telling a worried client to just buy the insurance policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stupid' rearranges SO INSURE, eight letters; it reads as an insult to the client.
explanation.definitionFit: A neurosis is a mental disorder marked by persistent worry or compulsive behaviour.

clue.text: Camp it might be, but it traditionally gets members back in action

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ... made by ..., slang for camp gay men, would be camp

definitions.text: it traditionally gets members back in action
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the monarch's address opening each session of Parliament, which brings MPs back to work

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is a joke on queen, slang for an effeminate gay man; the second is the State Opening of Parliament, where the monarch reads out the government's programme.
explanation.definitionFit: The monarch's address sets out the legislative programme at the start of each parliamentary session, so MPs return to business.

clue.text: Oath Nixon was fond of?

parts.note: the Watergate tape transcripts replaced each of Nixon's swear words with a bracketed note that it had been cut

explanation.walkthrough: Oath here is a swear word, not a sworn promise; the Watergate transcripts made Nixon's cursing famous through the phrase 'expletive deleted'.
explanation.definitionFit: A swear word is an oath in its profane sense, and the Watergate transcripts showed how often Nixon used them.

clue.text: Fergie's first rash outburst when Andy just started to get inside

indicators.note: tells us the single letter is placed within the jumbled word
an outburst bursts the word apart, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: only the start of the word is used, so its first letter

parts.note: Prince Andrew, Fergie's husband; his first letter is A

explanation.surface: The Duchess of York's first impetuous tantrum came as soon as Prince Andrew got through the door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outburst' rearranges RASH into SRAH; 'just started' gives A from Andy, and 'to get inside' puts it after the S. 'first' is the definition: Fergie's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Fergie is Sarah Ferguson, Duchess of York, so her first name, her forename, is the answer.

clue.text: Our political gossip bunged on thick?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Private Eye's own column of Westminster gossip
second meaning: the brown condiment, splodged liberally on food

explanation.walkthrough: HP Sauce is a British brown sauce for chips and fry-ups, and also the title of Private Eye's political gossip column, the HP being Houses of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: The bottled condiment is something people dollop on generously, and it names the magazine's column on Westminster tittle-tattle.

clue.text: By which perverse natural state bastards rule?

definitions.text: By which perverse natural state bastards rule?

parts.note: sods is British slang for unpleasant people, bastards
a law is a rule

explanation.surface: A sour question about what perverted constitution lets bastards govern the country.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a jibe at a government of bastards, Major's word for his Eurosceptic rebels; the whole clue also describes the principle that whatever can go wrong will.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying that anything which can go wrong will do so describes the world's perverse natural tendency.

clue.text: True-blue supporters?

parts.note: true-blue means staunchly Conservative, blue being the Tory colour, and the loyal grass-roots members are known by this phrase

explanation.walkthrough: True-blue is British slang for a staunch Conservative, and the three words name a party's loyal rank-and-file.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes the loyal rank-and-file members of a political party who back it whatever happens.

clue.text: Chuck out somewhat snide Portillo!

indicators.note: only some of the letters are used, so the answer is found inside the words

parts.note: the answer is in snidE PORTillo

explanation.surface: A call to expel the sneering Michael Portillo, the right-wing Tory cabinet minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somewhat' says only part of 'snide Portillo' is used. Michael Portillo was a Eurosceptic Conservative minister in John Major's cabinet.
explanation.definitionFit: To expel a person from a country is to throw them out, informally to chuck them out.

clue.text: See 5
Eurosceptic malevolent Conservative inside party

indicators.note: says that the other pieces go within the word for party

parts.note: a bash is informal for a party
ill as an adjective means hostile or harmful, as in ill will

explanation.surface: A charge that an ill-willed Tory Europhobe is working against the party from within.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' signals the container. Bill Cash was a leading Conservative Eurosceptic MP who fought the Maastricht Treaty.
explanation.definitionFit: Bill Cash MP was among the best-known Tory rebels hostile to European integration in the 1990s.

clue.text: Australia gets in personal stink with low grade plonk

indicators.note: Australia gets in alongside the stink, joining it in the charade

parts.note: BO is body odour
Oz is the informal name for Australia
E is a low exam grade

explanation.surface: Australian wine dismissed as smelly cheap plonk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets in' only means Australia joins the stink side by side; it is not a container. Plonk is British slang for cheap wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Booze is any alcoholic drink, and plonk is cheap wine, a kind of booze.

clue.text: Harold's follower gives everybody a good high in jail

indicators.note: says that the pieces before it are put within the word for jail

parts.note: can is slang for prison
all means everybody
H is the abbreviation for high, as on pencils and taps

explanation.surface: A tale of whoever succeeded Harold handing round drugs in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives' is a link. Harold Wilson resigned as Prime Minister in 1976 and James Callaghan succeeded him.
explanation.definitionFit: James Callaghan succeeded Harold Wilson as Labour leader and Prime Minister in 1976.

clue.text: One who's better than all other men at howls of self-pity, we hear!

definitions.text: One who's better than all other men at howls of self-pity, we hear!

indicators.note: says the phrase is to be taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.words: One who's better than all other men at howls of self-pity
parts.note: a prince among men at wails, the champion self-pitying howler, is a prince of wails

explanation.surface: A mocking tribute to the nation's champion whinger.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'prince' is one better than all others, and wails are howls; 'we hear' turns 'prince of wails' into the title of Prince Charles, mocked for his self-pitying 1994 television interview.
explanation.definitionFit: The title held by the heir to the throne, Charles, who complained publicly about his unhappy upbringing and marriage.

clue.text: Be the first to show Heseletine's ultimately after Major's job

indicators.note: says the single letter comes after the other piece

parts.note: John Major was Prime Minister, also called the premier

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of the name is taken

parts.note: Michael Heseltine, misspelt in the clue; the name ends in E

explanation.surface: A hint that Michael Heseltine will eventually get John Major's job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' takes the last letter of the name and 'after' puts it behind PREMIER. Heseltine, Major's deputy and rival, was tipped to succeed him; the clue misspells his name.
explanation.definitionFit: To give the first public performance of a play or film is to premiere it.

clue.text: One who gives the board some stick, this minister?

definitions.text: One who gives the board some stick
definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who writes on a blackboard with a stick of chalk
second meaning: Lynda ..., Minister for Overseas Development

explanation.walkthrough: 'gives the board some stick' sounds like attacking company directors; it means writing with chalk on a blackboard. Lynda Chalker was a Conservative minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Baroness Chalker served in John Major's government as Minister for Overseas Development, and one who uses chalk is literally a chalker.

clue.text: EC fated to drift east? Shit!

indicators.note: letters left to drift wander out of their order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A Eurosceptic's curse at the European Community drifting eastward.
explanation.walkthrough: EC is the European Community. 'to drift' rearranges EC FATED plus E for east.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a verb, the vulgar word means to empty the bowels, which is what the answer means.

clue.text: Bough in female underwear with no central heating

parts.note: a bra is women's underwear
CH is the usual abbreviation for central heating in property listings

explanation.surface: Someone hiding a tree limb inside a bra in an unheated room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' and 'with' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A bough is a large limb of a tree, the same thing as a branch.

clue.text: Born to take the piss out of drug incentive

parts.note: to rib is to tease or mock, the meaning of the British slang take the piss
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: Someone apparently born to mock the drug-incentive scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take the piss out of' is British slang for mock.
explanation.definitionFit: A bribe is an inducement, money offered to persuade, so an incentive.

clue.text: Winnie not queer according to the general body of-Christians

indicators.note: not means the word for queer is left out

parts.note: Winnie was the nickname of Winston Churchill
queer in its old sense means unwell, ill

explanation.surface: Someone defending Churchill from a charge of homosexuality, claiming the backing of Christendom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes ILL; queer here means poorly, as in 'feeling queer'. 'according to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The church is the whole community of Christian believers taken together.

clue.text: Hallo! recruits Frost — possible high level seizure results!

indicators.note: the greeting takes on the next word as a new member of the team, joining it

parts.note: hi is a greeting, like hallo
Jack Frost is the personification of frost

explanation.surface: A greeting signs up David Frost, the interviewer, leading to a high-level coup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recruits' means the greeting takes Frost on as a partner, not inside it. Frost looks like David Frost the broadcaster, but it is Jack Frost, winter personified.
explanation.definitionFit: Hijacking an aircraft is a seizure that may take place at high altitude, so 'possible' covers that pun.

clue.text: Eggar's evidently concealing his true mouthpiece?

indicators.note: says the words hold the answer within them

parts.note: the answer is in eggARS Evidently

explanation.surface: A gibe that Tim Eggar, the Tory minister, is hiding who really speaks for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealing' says the answer lies within 'Eggar's evidently'. Tim Eggar was a Conservative minister; the joke is that he talks out of his backside.
explanation.definitionFit: To talk out of one's backside is to speak nonsense, so the rude word is cast as Eggar's real organ of speech.

clue.text: See 10
Sofa Mellor has celebrity in

indicators.note: the words have the answer in them, held inside

parts.note: the answer is in soFA MEllor

explanation.surface: David Mellor, the minister of sofa-romping notoriety, has brought a famous person in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has ... in' says 'Sofa Mellor' holds the answer. David Mellor resigned in 1992 after tabloid stories of an affair with an actress.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrity is the state of being well known, which is fame.

clue.text: Sort out booze — it'll give the speaker a lift

definitions.text: it'll give the speaker a lift

indicators.note: sorting something out shuffles it, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

parts.note: rum is a spirit, a kind of booze

explanation.surface: An instruction to arrange the drinks, which will cheer up whoever's talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges SORT to ROST.
explanation.definitionFit: A rostrum is a raised platform, so it lifts a speaker above the audience.

clue.text: He's no plonker

parts.note: plonker is British slang both for a fool and for the penis; this man lacks the second

explanation.walkthrough: 'He's no plonker' sounds like praise for someone's sense; plonker is British slang for a fool, and also for the penis.
explanation.definitionFit: A castrated man has lost his genitals, so he literally has no plonker.
